content:
I'll be the first to admit that my modified iPhone camera looks pretty ridiculous — but it actually makes using my iPhone for photography more practical and a lot more fun.

The modification was originally my solution to a problem I encountered while filming a video, but I've since found myself using it far more often than I ever expected…

One of the biggest divides in the compact camera world is whether or not a camera has a viewfinder. Incidentally, old-school camera enthusiasts used to get very worked up about the merits and drawbacks of electronic viewfinders (EVFs) versus optical ones, but EVFs are now so good that basically nobody cares anymore.

But regardless of whether it's optical or electronic, a viewfinder offers very practical benefits over composing with the rear screen, especially when shooting in bright sunlight. Even with the screen brightness turned up to maximum, it's really hard to see what you're shooting in harsh sunlight, and you may also have to deal with reflections on the screen.

Although in London this has never really been a major issue, this summer brought a record-breaking heatwave, and frankly, I feel like the last time I saw a cloud or some rain was about thirty years ago.

But to me, it means more than just that. I also feel that seeing only what's in the frame when you compose gives a different psychological sensation from seeing everything around you. Sometimes it's precisely because of that immersion that I choose to use a dedicated camera rather than my iPhone.

When I was choosing a camera for video a few years ago, the Blackmagic Pocket Cinema Camera 4K was clearly the top choice at the time, but the lack of a viewfinder gave me pause. In the end, I decided it wasn't a major issue for me, because I'd mainly be using it indoors, and when I needed it outside, attaching a large screen with a sun hood would solve most of the problems.

However, there are also times when I want to use it without lugging around the camera plus the screen as one big rig, so I found a simple accessory suitable for outdoor use. This accessory is a two-in-one sun hood and magnifying glass design that magnetically attaches to the camera's rear screen, effectively providing an optical viewfinder.

I was about to have a shoot where I'd need to film with both the BMPCC 4K and my iPhone 16 Pro Max. I went to the location and did a quick test shoot, and found that the viewfinder accessory really helped. Because the BMPCC 4K and iPhone screens are very close in size, I wondered whether this accessory might also work on the iPhone.

Of course, the iPhone doesn't have magnetic attachment built in, but the iPhone is light enough that manually holding it against the magnifier is no problem at all. To my surprise, this method works amazingly well, especially when I use the Camera Control button as the shutter.

Since then, I've found myself using it to take photos in quite a few situations, enjoying the convenience of being able to see the screen more easily in harsh sunlight, as well as that sense of immersion. My iPhone has been my primary camera for several years now, and with this DIY modification, I feel even more that there are plenty of occasions where a phone alone is more than enough.

Genius or idiot? Let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you agree with the latter, unfortunately the product I bought seems to have been discontinued, and I haven't seen any similar products specifically designed for screens larger than three inches. If you find one, be sure to share a link in the comments.
